I had existing solar and went all out to fully electrify the house so i got Solargain to install a battery, hot water service and ev charger. Things started well, even the install was pretty smooth - then the wheels fell off. Zero support to rectify issues with the system. The hot water system doesn't communicate with their app - even though their website says it does. The system wasn't properly installed so no DLR function for the EV charger. The app also claims to show real time data - but it doesn't come even close - you have to force the app closed and relaunch it to get updated data. They don't respond and are just fobbing us off with excuses. They also wont remove the zero export limit, despite us having an agreement for export in place with the network operator. In a nutshell,  the system isn't whats advertised or what was sold. Solargain, once they have your money are difficult to deal with and I do not recommend them. Solargain shoild be avoided.

This was immediately reported to Solargain who promised a quick fix from their subcontractor. From here, Solargain management were unable have their subcontractor actually effect the repairs for several months, seemingly unable to get him to return their calls. Additionally Solargain were unwilling for me to have the damage repaired by my own contractor, with Solargain paying the bill.Unfortunately I cannot recommend Solargain due to their poor practice of subcontracting their jobs - there is no guarantee that this established company can actually provide a competent installer!

MY SOLAR STORYI was looking for non-premium 6.6kw solar system. I took the view that Solar systems are evolving; noting the development in Australia of improved and more cost effective solar panels and that, in all likelihood, I would not be in my home in 25 years. Thus, a 25 year warranty and premium panels etc was unnecessary. I wanted an efficient effective system that would last, say, 10 years.A quote was obtained from eight suppliers. Suppliers were vetted and culled using  their ABN and ASIC records, a search of their address (Google earth etc), attempting to contact them by telephone, CEC membership check, electrical licence check, internet search for any supplier media or supplier reviews; e.g. ProductReview, Facebook, Whirlpool, Choice and SolarQuotes.As regards the quotes-Some suppliers:-quoted around the $3200 price for a 6.66kw system, wanted $100 deposit, wanted final payment days before installation, would not accept payment upon installation/with proper system operation, constantly telephoned seeking quote acceptance, “1300” telephone number never answered, address was seen to be a mail drop box in QLD or found to be a $49 a month office mail address in NSW, had minimal if any customer reviews, had lost their licence and were under Government scrutiny, in my view appeared to be using unskilled labour, had changed its name recently, had  commenced within the past year or so and seemed unlikely to be in existence in years to come so as to carry out labour warranty.  All these suppliers seemed to use what could be called “boiler room” sales staff keen to get the next sale- on a number of occasions I thought I was speaking to persons overseas.Other suppliers:-quoted $3700-$4100 for a 6.66kw system, did not require a deposit, gave a pensioner discount, offered to price match within reason, had significant (=> 25 favourable reviews), had existed as the one entity for at least 3 years, had one or several physical business addresses/warehouse and appeared more likely to provide future warranty etc service. Some of these suppliers disapproved of the cheap quotes and warned that warranty might be an issue as well as product/installation quality.As to the solar product, the panel and inverter specifications-efficiency etc were examined via, for example SolarQuotes. The Retail Prices (including GST) of panels and inverters was obtained to enable the forming of some opinion on supplier pricing. (see for example solarshoponline.com.au)  The background of the panel and inverter suppliers was reviewed. An Australian office for each panel and inverter supplier was sought where warranty claims could be lodged.Over time, I selected one type of panel and inverter and then obtained a quote from suppliers; together with each supplier’s Contract/Terms and Conditions, based upon my selected panel and inverter items.The Contract/Terms and Conditions of all suppliers was examined and all had issues, such as poor english expression, referencing non- existent clauses, obscure provisions and broadly stating that product substitution might be necessary, along with changes to the quoted price and the value of  STC’s, albeit with some provision for customer approval. All suppliers were asked to verify they held, or had ready access to, panels and inverters. One supplier said it had to source product.The STC rebate offered by suppliers varied markedly due to the use of an “STC” value from $30 to the maximum of $40. This resulted in the total STC rebate offered on a 6.6kw system comprising 18 * 370K panels, could be between $2761 and $3681.It is of note that a customer can pay the full quoted price for a solar system to a solar supplier; ex the STC rebate and then the customer themselves can apply separately and be paid the STC rebate.I was warned to check the bona fides of suppliers offering cheap solar pricing.  I accepted that advice, but took the view the risk of contracting with such a supplier could be accepted from the point of view the cash saved (maybe $900) could cover any future installer labour cost not covered by what might then be a non-existent supplier warranty.That notwithstanding, I culled suppliers by requiring 25 favourable reviews, a business existence of  2 years, a land line that responded and a verifiable physical address. None of the cheaper quotes survived that cull.The chosen supplier (Solargain) had warehoused stock, significant favourable reviews, offered full payment upon installation, had CEC membership, had physical location(s), was contactable by telephone, corporate existence for =>3 years, demonstrated associations/business relations with large corporates, demonstrated experience in large commercial/residential solar installations, provided acceptable warranty assurances and on balance, was most likely to install a fully operational contracted solar product on time and on budget.As a result, I paid (through the nose you might say) roughly $3900 (no pensioner rebate though) for a 6.66kw system with 18*370kw Trina panels and a Growatt 5kw inverter (5+5 year warranty). The next best price was around $3750. I did not research prices for the racking.I arranged for Solargain to conduct a site inspection to confirm where the solar panels would be placed and that my switch board specs etc were satisfactory. My switchboard was upgraded to incorporate “RCD’s” (Residual Current Devices- a safety mechanism) and additional neutral wiring.The site inspection resulted in a price increase to allow for 15metres of extra cabling (said to be due to possible difficulty in the roof cavity) and a switchboard upgrade that I arranged for separately at a cost of $500.I accepted Solargain’s quote on 4/11 and on 30/11 the system was installed and up and running with my property tidied up in around 6 hours. Solargain did all the paperwork. Polite,tidy, punctual installation team.I hope all this helps in your solar search.

First of all, I would express my thanks Finn, for the great help your website was to me in sorting out the best option for me to follow. In my case I had an existing 1.5KW system already installed on the prime NE facing position, that had been around for a while (110 Watt panels and an early model SunnyBoy inverter, production of which has been discontinued) so that increased the range of alternatives to consider and the factors (both physical and financial)  to weigh up. You can take for granted that you are going to lose your 44 cent FIT.  There seems to be a lot of at times somewhat hysterical misunderstanding around about that.  If you are getting a 44 cent FIT, that only applies to the relatively low qty of exported kwh after any self-consumption from your current system. Even if you consume those few kwh,  you are still saving nearly 26 cents anyway because you are not drawing power from the grid in respect of them.  Your guess is as good as mine as to what the level of future tariffs is going to be, and how quickly the present gap of 18 cents will narrow over the next few years.Overall I was very happy with my choice of Solar Gain. To cut a long story short one of the original installers mislabelled the hand-drawn array map and so the wrong microinverter (a working one) was replaced.  After a few phone calls to Solargain and Enphase support and then a letter to Solargain, Solargain decided to send someone out. The same technician arrived this morning and between us we realized the mistake of the original installers. He then fixed the correct faulty microinverter (loose wire rather than an actual fault). I then went back into the Enphase software array builder and updated our system with all the correct details.Overall I'm happy except for the fact that it took numerous calls then a letter to Solargain to convince them that they hadn't fixed the problem correctly.
